prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic fluctuations, providing the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed in one respect. I now propose Kiyotaki and Moore alone for B002 and no longer add Gertler. The scientific case for the part is unchanged. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a tractable general-equilibrium mechanism in which borrowing limits tied to asset values turn temporary shocks into large, persistent fluctuations. It is conceptually original, has nearly three decades of theoretical, quantitative and policy use, and the 2008 crisis made its relevance widely visible. It has a clean two-author origin. The exchange changed my view on Gertler for three reasons. First, the accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke, who is already a laureate, so a citation naming Gertler invites a dispute about who the other originators are, including Gilchrist. Second, Gertler's credit is split between B002 and the eight-name B043. Third, in round 1 I argued that his later intermediary-based quantitative work is separable from the 2022 recognition. On reflection that is a claim about a different, later achievement. It should be judged on its own merits and not attached to the collateral-constraint citation to widen its scope. I cannot support it from the record before me beyond my own recollection. B002 is a stronger candidate as a bounded two-name credit, and my preference does not rest on how many members ranked it first. I keep B002 ahead of B012 and B025 for the originality of the mechanism, its reach into macro theory, quantitative models and policy practice, and the clarity of credit. This is a close judgment against B012 in particular, and I do not treat it as settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig on banks and financial crises. I believe the mechanisms are distinct, but that is a judgment and not an established fact. The second reservation is empirical. The quantitative size of collateral-driven amplification is less cleanly identified than the theory's influence suggests, and my own preference for B002 partly rests on conceptual weight over measurement. Third, narrowing to two names leaves the financial-accelerator and intermediary strands unrecognised, so the citation may look narrower than the literature that followed. A Committee that places measurement and confirmed use above conceptual originality would reasonably prefer B012 or B025. Finally, I am the chair, and I wrote the first-round summary. Its counts of explicit supporters describe positions only and are not evidence of merit.

responses.point: Krusell narrowed to Kiyotaki and Moore after Hjalmarsson's argument. He says the accelerator lineage has other originators, one already a laureate, that Gertler's credit is split with B043, and that he would revisit Gertler only for a broader citation on financial frictions in monetary transmission.
responses.response: I accept this and have made the same move. The chair's summary asked what separates Gertler's intermediary-based work from the 2022 recognition. I cannot give decisive evidence for that separation from the materials before the Committee. I only have my own reading, and that is not enough to justify a third name against the attribution risks you describe. I also agree that a broader financial-frictions prize would be a different citation and would need its own case, probably alongside B043 in a monetary-policy context. For this slate I treat the two-name collateral-constraint credit as the defensible unit. I note that you and I are long-time co-authors and both prefer B002, so the Committee should not treat our agreement as independent confirmation.

responses.point: Teorell proposes two parts: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012. This keeps within the three-person cap and covers a mechanism and a method. He records that Pakes-alone omits Berry and Levinsohn and that the pairing has no obvious shared theme. His fallback is B002 with Gertler as a single part.
responses.response: I do not support the two-part version, and the reasons are mainly attributional. Pakes alone leaves out Berry and Levinsohn, whom you call a real loss. If B012 were chosen on the merits, I would want the BLP trio, and under the three-person cap that cannot be combined with a two-name B002. The pairing also adds no scientific strength to B002, since the cap forces the B012 part to be weaker. A single focused part is cleaner. I also note that your fallback of B002 with Gertler is the version I am now giving up, for the credit-split and lineage reasons you gave me in your own round-1 reply. If you move toward the two-name B002, that closes much of the remaining gap between our positions on this ballot.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first. He would credit B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore alone and says Gertler's inclusion blurs the citation. He also says the support count for B002 does not settle the merit comparison with B012.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and the support count does not enter my reasoning. On mechanism versus method, the chair's summary asks which criterion should decide. I do not think either alone should. I look for a discovery with a clear origin, durable use across fields, and confirmation over time. B012 does better on confirmation and on the breadth of applied use. B002 does better on the originality of the idea and on the clarity of credit. What would move me is evidence that collateral amplification is quantitatively small or not robust, and the record before me contains none. My ranking therefore rests on the weight I give conceptual originality, and I hold that weight loosely. I would support B012 as the BLP trio if the Committee judged measurement and applied reach to outweigh it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B012 first with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. She calls the BLP core compact, treats B002 as her main fallback with Kiyotaki and Moore alone, and says Bresnahan's omission is a real weakness unless the citation is worded narrowly.
responses.response: Your argument against adding Gertler to B002 influenced my change, and I thank you for it. On B012 I find the BLP attribution compact and the maturity beyond doubt. The Bresnahan problem is real. If his contribution were judged equal in kind to the demand-estimation breakthrough, no three-person set would be fully defensible. I read it differently from you only slightly: I think a narrowly worded citation on demand estimation for differentiated products and dynamic industry models can be defended, with the omissions recorded openly. That is why B012 is my second alternative and not a minor one. My remaining difference is the weight I give to conceptual originality over measurement tools, and I accept this is a legitimate difference in judgment and not a factual dispute.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B025 first with Helpman and Melitz and B002 second. She would not add Gertler, because of the Bernanke lineage and the B043 overlap. She concedes the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a real attribution risk and notes that confirmation of collateral amplification is thinner than the firm-level evidence for B025.
responses.response: I agree with you on Gertler and agree that firm-level evidence on selection and reallocation is stronger than the evidence on the size of collateral amplification. That is a real asymmetry. The chair's summary also asks for a consistent principle on prize adjacency. I would treat adjacency as a duplication test, meaning whether the specific discovery was already credited, and not as a merit criterion or a balance device. Applied consistently, I judge the 2022 prize (banks and runs) to be a different mechanism from collateral-constraint amplification, the 2008 prize (scale economies and trade patterns) to be different from firm selection, and the 2024 prize to be a different outcome from fiscal policy in B050. Each of these is a judgment, and I hold the 2008 case for B025 with the same uncertainty as the 2022 case for B002. The omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is the part I find hardest to resolve for B025, and I treat it as the reason B025 remains my alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises covers the collateral-constraint mechanism. I judge the mechanisms distinct, but that is not established.
Whether the quantitative size of collateral-driven amplification is large enough to justify the weight I give the mechanism. I know of no evidence in the record that settles this.
Whether the Committee weighs conceptual originality above measurement and applied reach when comparing B002 with B012. My ordering depends on this weight.

Whether the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin undermines B012, and whether that of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum undermines B025. I rely on recollection and have not verified relative credit independently.
Whether leaving Gertler and Gilchrist out of B002 makes the citation look narrower than the literature, and where Gertler's separate contribution is best assessed.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. I chair the Committee and wrote the round-1 summary. None of the credited names in my preferred part, Kiyotaki and Moore, or in my alternatives is among my listed co-authors or connections, and I no longer propose Gertler. I am a frequent co-author and IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart, who both prefer B002, and I co-authored a 2026 paper with Friberg. None of them is a candidate. Their agreement with me should not be read as independent confirmation. My macroeconomics background makes B002 adjacent to my own field, and I have topical affinity with political economy (B050) and social mobility (B015), neither of which is in my configuration or alternatives. I disclose these without adjudicating them.
